newsitem.title: UK: Rating cut shows Turkey faces econ crisis - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Rating cut shows Turkey faces econ crisis - analysts.

text.p: A cut in Turkey's investment rating is yet another sign of serious problems facing the country, and analysts on Monday warned of a crisis unless the fractious government makes a real effort to reform the economy.
The Turkish stock market tumbled nearly four percent after the downgrading last Friday by Standard and Poor's of the country's long-term foreign currency rating.
S&P cited worsening fiscal and debt service pressures, making Turkey even more vulnerable to changes in investor confidence.
"It is very serious...it will get much worse before it gets better," said Susanne Hallergard, analyst with ING Barings.
The lower rating is the latest blow to Turkey's weak coalition government which analysts say has repeatedly failed to come up with serious economic reforms.
Clear signs of change are crucial if Islamist Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan has a chance of winning over the International Montary Fund.
Late last week, a court ruling blocked a law that would allow his government to sell state property from which it had hoped to raise about $3.0 billion.
Some analysts warned against seeing a repeat of the currency crisis which hit Turkey last time S&P announced a downgrading two years ago, noting the central bank had $17 billion in currency reserves.

"The downgrading in itself won't make a huge difference. But what I am worried about is that it is yet more confirmation that the international markets believe the government is not doing enough. There is a lack of structural reforms," he added.
But he wondered whether S&P's move would be enough to push the government into action. "Unless the economy gets really bad, the coalition won't force itself to do something," he said.
The downgrading will certainly force up Turkey's cost of foreign borrowing at a time when it is trying to raise more money much more cheaply overseas.

The shift to cheaper but riskier foreign borrowing, an increasingly large current account deficit and high borrowing levels are signals of a crisis, said Miranda Xafa, a senior economist at Salomon Brothers.
"These are early warning signs that something may happen," she said, adding the government is now scraping the bottom of the barrel to find ways to get finance.
"So far the government hasn't delivered on any of the reforms except privatisation," Xafa said.
But that will not work unless there are permanent cuts in spending and an increase in government revenue, she added.
